en: Preface to the *Jianzhou Hongshi Lu*:
When I was composing the *Quwu*, I traveled through Fuzhou and learned that Jianzhou was a reservoir of the School of Principle (*Lixue*).

Later, upon reading various texts of the *Chuan deng lu*, I further learned that Jianzhou was also a reservoir of the School of Chan (*Chanxue*). Whenever I encountered a monk from Jianzhou, I invariably inquired about [these matters].
The former virtuous men of our district—though often unable to answer [my inquiries]—therefore left me in a state of deep melancholy for a long time.
In the spring of the Ding-si year, my younger brother Yongjue first abandoned Confucianism to enter the Buddhist path and studied "withered Chan" under the late Master Shouchang.

Consequently, I discussed those former virtuous men of our district with him at great length; they were all as pure as polished jade and as noble as soaring phoenixes and peacocks—qualities far beyond anything I had previously encountered.
When I learned of this, I was overjoyed. Pointing to my chest, I said, "This is the *History of the Sangha in One Section*.

The Master replied, "I shall record it and transmit it. Not long after, the former master passed away. The Master came to Boshan and lived there with me for five years. During that time, I occasionally pressed him on his previous promise.
He said, "Wait until you can recognize your own nostrils, and then I will do it. Later, he returned to Min and lived in seclusion at Mount Yun.
Communicating news: In the spring of the Wuchen year, I returned from Gushan to Boshan. On the way, I passed through Jianzhou, where the Master welcomed me at Kaiyuan Temple.
I looked at him and recognized him, saying, "Now you can be considered a monk of Jianzhou. The Master smiled but did not answer.
I then asked, "Have you swept the tomb of Shouchang yet? The Master replied, "As for sweeping, it has not been neglected; it is simply..."
He did not wish for others to know. I said, "You have stolen the broom. The Master asked, "And what about you, Preceptor?
I replied, "The sweeping is not abandoned; it is simply that I have never moved it. The Master said, "Then the Preceptor has not stolen the broom either?
Thereupon we laughed and parted. In the winter of the Jisi year, a letter arrived at Boshan from Zhi Cheng, a monk from Jianzhou, who had sent it.

I shall provide a preface for this work. Having examined the collection he has assembled, I find it divided into four sections: the first is titled "Reaching the Root," which re-clarifies the fundamental principle;
the second is "Manifesting Transformation," which demonstrates the efficacy of prayers; the third is "Honoring Virtue," which records various practices;

and the fourth is "Aiding the Teaching," which serves as a golden wall and moat for the Dharma. Taken together, the work is entitled *Hongshi Chongfahua* (Extending the Buddha’s Teachings and Honoring the Transformation of the Dharma).
His understanding was correct, his arguments were definitive, his research was extensive, and his classifications were rigorous; was he not a worthy historian?

In the past, Daoxuan composed the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha) during the Tang dynasty; yet he lacked literary skill and was unaware of the existence of the *Biqiuni zhuan* (Biographies of Nuns).
He categorized the Dharma lineage of Bodhidharma among those of withered and silent asceticism—how dark was his insight! Zanning, however, composed the *Sengshi*.

In the Song dynasty, [the compiler] possessed great learning yet lacked talent; for he ranked Huangbo under "Responsive Communion" (Gantong), ranked Yantou under "Relinquishing the Body" (Yishen), and ranked Yongming under "Promoting Merit" (Xingfu).
As for Yunmen—the sovereign among monks—he instead omitted him and failed to include him.
Thus, his errors were all the more egregious. Juefan followed with a eulogy and a preface; his style was lofty, elegant, brilliant, and clear, ascending to the platform of the masters.
Yet, it recorded only the eminent figures of the Chan school—can this truly be called a comprehensive history?

Although the Master’s current ambition covers merely a single province, Xuan-ning acknowledged its refined appropriateness, and Juefan commended its completeness; it stands far above [all others] alone.
He emerged; before him there was no creator. By this alone, one may discern the master’s peerless rank.

Moreover, those of a thousand years past relied upon the master to transmit [the teachings], and those of a thousand years hence rely upon the master to understand them. Thus, the master’s merit surely lies both above and below the span of a thousand years.
Among those in Jianzhou who are called propagators of the Śākya, who could it be other than the master? For this reason, I am delighted.
Observing its completion, I have composed this preface without hesitation. Furthermore, I have heard that the Master’s writings are exceedingly abundant;
it would be fitting to carve them all onto bamboo slips for transmission. If this were to happen, the world and future generations would be profoundly benefited—not merely the Jianzhou region alone.
I request that others wipe their eyes and await this.
On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment in the winter of the Jisi year of the Chongzhen era, written by the monk Da Yi of Boshan as a preface to the *Hongshi lu*.

While returning south on leave, I passed through Tanyang. I heard that there was a man named Master Jue in this district who, having been enrolled as a scholar at a young age, immediately severed all ties to sound and form and abandoned all worldly amusements.
He devoted his mind entirely to pure karma; he later shaved his head under the guidance of Wuming of Shouchang and took Wuyi as his companion.
Day by day, they exhorted one another regarding the supreme Way. Recently, he has established a great Dharma center.
Regarding the *Chuang* (Banner) at Mount He: Jianzhou was anciently known as the "Dharma Cave" (*dharmaguhā*), yet its historical records are largely deficient.

Therefore, having examined various texts, I have compiled this unique "eccentric history" entitled the *Hongshilu* (Record of the Propagation of Buddhism). It consists of four sections: the Record of the Fundamental [Teaching], the Record of Manifestation, the Record of Transformation, and the Record of Venerable Virtue.
He resolved to assist the teaching, and thus the Dharma lamp of Jianzhou was rekindled by Master Jue. He established a lifelong friendship with my disciple Wei Qufei;
I rejoiced at being able to encounter him in person. Consequently, I sighed and said: "The Way does not travel in vain; it is man who can propagate the Way.
At this time, when the Buddhist teachings are declining, Master Jue’s understanding and practice serve as a means to propagate and instruct others.

Thus he graces the world; it is only fitting that those who would "hasten with satchel in hand" [to follow him] should come from all over the South. Furthermore, his verse in response to his nephews contains the lines:
"My backbone has been cast from raw iron since birth; though called a hundred thousand times, I do not turn my head.

From these words, one knows without asking that he has realized the fundamental source, honored virtue, and manifested the transformative power of the Way, bearing it all upon his single shoulder. It is truly he who has elucidated the deeds of the ancient worthies.

His profound illumination serves as a model for future generations; is he not truly worthy of being called a "Perfectly Awakened One"? Written in the autumn of the Xinwei year by He Qiaoyuan of Wenling, this is the preface to the *Record of the Propagation of Buddhism in Jianzhou*.
The *Hongshi lu* (Records of the Propagation and Exegesis) is a compilation of those who were able to propagate and explain the Way of the Śākya clan.

Since this Way was first revealed through the dream of the Golden Man and the White Horse arrived from the West, there have been successive authors throughout the generations who have greatly propagated its teachings.

Consequently, like a thousand lamps vying to shine, their brilliance has illuminated both the present and the past; it is vast and grand beyond reckoning. As for our own land, prior to the Six Dynasties, there was generally no such record.

I have heard that when the Tang dynasty first flourished, Buddhist monasteries were initially established. It was from the time Mazu entered the Guanzhong region and began his transformative teachings at Fojie Ling in Jianyang that Chan studies first began to spread widely.
Subsequently, although the Chan and doctrinal schools diverged as distinct traditions and the teachings on *xing* (nature) and *xiang* (phenomena) differed in their tenets, [the tradition continued].
Together, you were able to cause the wind of profound transformation to blow and the fountain of the Dharma to gush forth like arrows; all of you were the ferries and bridges for our Śākya clan.
Yet, since the rise of the Ming dynasty, more than two hundred years have passed; the lamp of the school has lost its flame and the ocean of the teachings has likewise been submerged.
Only here and there are two or three remaining, sparse as morning stars. To whom, then, shall the responsibility for propagating the Way be entrusted? — From Xiantan County.
I am but a vulgar man who has unworthily entered the ranks of the black-robed clergy and found refuge in the Dharma cave.

Although a firefly’s light cannot illuminate much and my own skills are utterly deficient, my single-minded devotion to antiquity is ever keen within my foolish heart. When I gaze up at the exemplary figures of the past, I cannot help but shed tears.
Thus I reflect: these are the same rivers and mountains of old; these are the same sun and moon. Today, too, these are the same rivers and mountains; today, too, these are the same sun and moon.
Is this person alone different from those of antiquity? Why is it that the dharma-gates have become so desolate and silent, such that the gap between the present and the past has become so vast?

Is it perhaps because the former traces have vanished, leaving no basis for contemplation and inspiration? Or is it because people are so habituated to their recent practices that there is no one to rouse them?
For these reasons, I, disregarding my own limited ignorance, have extensively explored the various scriptures and drawn from the teachings of the masters.
Those who produced [this work] in Jian, or those who opened the Dharma and manifested its transformation in Jian, have all been recorded and transmitted.
This is so that students of later generations may see such hardship, such solemnity and caution, such vastness, and such far-reaching attainment of the ancients.
If they can suddenly change their course and advance toward the goal, then—
That the prosperity of the Tang and Song dynasties might perhaps be seen again today—this too cannot yet be known. Alas! Every person can become a Yao or a Shun;
the words of Master Mencius (Zi Yu) are certainly not deceptive. It is simply that for those with resolve, their undertakings will ultimately succeed.

If one is merely content with self-comfort and strictly limits oneself with self-satisfaction, then even if the various Patriarchs were to stand solemnly before one and issue a command, that person would [fail].
Turning their heads away, they pay it no heed. What, then, is the value of this record? As for the practice of this record, I wish to share it with those who possess the resolve. At this time...

Reaching the Source, Part One (Total: thirty-two persons).
To recognize the mind and reach its source is what first earns one the title of *śramaṇa*. The mind cannot be known; the eye does not see the eye.

It is beyond both conceptual understanding and realization, yet this title is established as a provisional designation. Entering the ocean of all Buddhas—this is the foremost. This is the aspiration to reach the source.
△ Chan Master Daoyi of Fojiling on Jianyang Mountain in Tang. A native of Shifang in Hanzhou, his surname was Ma.
His appearance was extraordinary; he walked like an ox and gazed like a tiger. He could extend his tongue past his nose, and beneath both soles were the marks of wheels.
In his youth, he followed Master Tang at Zizhou to receive the tonsure. During the Kaiyuan era, he practiced *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) at the Chuanfa Monastery on Mount Heng. Relying on...

Upon hearing this, the Upādhyāya recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and went to guide him; he subsequently attained realization of the secret intent. Later, he entered Min and resided at Fojie Ling in Jianyang.
At that time, the monks of Min had long been mired in gradualist and expedient teachings; upon suddenly hearing the sudden teaching, they all turned toward it with great enthusiasm.
Ganquan Zhixian, Qianqing Mingjue, and others were the first to rely upon him, eventually becoming great vessels of the Way. Thus it was.
He moved to Mount Gongong in Nan’gang, where his Chan teachings flourished extensively. One hundred and thirty-nine people succeeded him in the Dharma.

Upon his death, he was posthumously titled "Great Tranquility" (Daji), and his stupa was named "Great Adornment" (Dazhuangyan). It is said that the Chan school of the Seven Min regions truly originated with this master.
(Fojie Ling is now the Shengji Temple.)
△ During the Jian’an era of the Tang dynasty, there was the Chan Master Dazhu Huikai, whose secular surname was Zhu.
He received his training under the Venerable Zhi of Dayun Monastery in Yuezhou. Initially, he visited Chan Master Daoyi. Daoyi asked, “Where have you come from?
He replied, “I have come from Dayun Monastery in Yuezhou. Daoyi asked, “What do you intend to seek by coming here? He replied, “I seek the Buddha-dharma. Daoyi said, “In my place here...”
"There is not a single thing. What Dharma do you seek? You neglect your own precious treasury and wander about, abandoning your home—why do you do this?
He asked, "Which one is the treasure-trove of Huihai? The Master said, "That which is asking me right now is your treasure-trove.
It is fully complete with nothing lacking. Its use is sovereign; why rely on seeking it elsewhere? The Master spoke these words.
Realizing that his original mind was not attained through intellectual cognition, he prostrated himself with great joy and gratitude. He served as a disciple for six years.
Later, because his preceptor had grown old, he returned home abruptly to provide for him. Thereupon, he concealed his traces and hidden his talents, outwardly appearing dull and mute.

He composed the *Tunwu rudao yaomen lun* (A Treatise on the Essential Gate of Sudden Enlightenment to Entering the Way) in one fascicle. His dharma-nephew Xuanyan secretly brought it out to the region beyond the Yangtze River to present to Daoyi. Daoyi—
Having finished his reading, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In Yuezhou there is a great pearl, perfectly round and bright, its light penetrating freely without obstruction.
Among the crowd was one who knew the Master’s surname was Zhu; they urged him to go to Yue to seek him out and rely upon him. The Master said to him:
"O Zen guest, I do not understand Zen, nor do I possess a single dharma to show to others. Do not trouble yourself by standing here so long; please depart for now."

He retired [to rest]. At that time, his disciples gradually increased in number, and they pressed him with questions day and night. Having no other choice, he answered each question as it was posed; his eloquence was unimpeded.
On one occasion, several Dharma masters came to visit him and said, "We intend to pose a question. Will you respond to us?"

The Master said, "It is like the moon’s reflection in a deep pool; you may grasp it as you please. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "In this clear conversation face-to-face, who is not the Buddha?
The assembly was all at a loss. After a long while, the monk asked again, "With what Dharma do you teach and deliver people?"
The Master said, "I have never possessed a single dharma to save people. The monk replied, "This is how it is throughout the Chan masters' houses.

The Master then asked, "Virtuous One, what dharma do you preach to save people? He replied, "I lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Master asked, "How many lectures have you given so far?
He replied, "More than twenty. The Master asked, "By whom was this sutra spoken? The monk raised his voice and said, "Master, you are mocking me!"
"Do you not know that this was spoken by the Buddha? The Master said, "If one says that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma, they slander the Buddha;
such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught. If one says that this sutra was not spoken by the Buddha, they slander the sutra.
Please, Venerable Sir, speak on it. The monk had no reply. After a short while, the Master asked again, "The sutra says: 'If one views [the Buddha] by means of form...'"
"I seek the Tathāgata by means of sounds; such a person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata. "Virtuous One, tell me then: which one is the Tathāgata?
He replied, "When I arrived here, I was instead lost. The Master said, "You have never awakened from the beginning; how can you speak of being 'lost'?
He requested, "I pray that the Chan Master will explain this for me. The Master said, "Virtuous One, you have lectured on the sutras for more than twenty assemblies."

Yet you do not recognize the Tathāgata. The monk bowed and said, "I pray that you will grant me instruction. The Master said, "The 'Tathāgata' is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.
How could you have forgotten this? The monk said, "It is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. The Master said, "Virtuous One, even this is not yet it.
The monk said, "The scriptural text is clear; how can it be 'not yet it'? The Master asked, "Virtuous One, are you such? The monk said, "Such. The Master said, "..."
"Are wood and stone like this? he asked. The monk replied, "They are. The Master said, "Great Virtue, are you like wood and stone? The monk replied, "There is no difference.
The Master said, "In what way do you differ from wood and stone? The monk was speechless for a long while, and then asked, "How does one attain Great Nirvana?
The Master said, "By not creating the karma of birth and death. The monk asked, "What is the karma of birth and death? The Master said, "Seeking Great Nirvana."
"Attaching to 'is' is the karma of birth and death. Abandoning defilement to grasp purity is the karma of birth and death. Having attainment and realization is the karma of birth and death.
Not being liberated from the gates of antidotes is the karma of birth and death. He asked, "How then can one attain liberation?

The Master said, "Originally there has been no bondage; there is no need to seek liberation. To act directly and walk straight is that which is unequaled. He asked, "Master, you are like a harmonizer."
"Truly, this is rare indeed," he said, bowing in gratitude and departing. A practitioner asked, "Regarding 'this very mind is Buddha,' which one is the Buddha?
The Master said, "Which one do you suspect is not the Buddha? Point it out. The practitioner had no reply. The Master said, "To realize it, everything within the sphere of perception is it;
if you do not awaken to it, you will remain forever alienated and distant. The Vinaya Master Faming said to the Master, "In the house of the Chan masters..."

"You have fallen into emptiness," the Master said. "In fact, it is you, Master of the Dharma-seats, who have fallen into emptiness. Mingda was greatly startled and asked, "How could one fall into emptiness?

The Master replied, "The sutras and treatises are but paper, ink, and written characters. Since paper, ink, and written characters are all empty, even if one establishes dharmas such as names and phrases based upon sounds, they are none other than empty.
You, Master of the Dharma-seats, cling to the substance of the teachings; how then can you not fall [into emptiness]?"
Kongming asked, "Does Master Chan fall into emptiness? The Master said, "I do not fall into emptiness. Kongming asked, "How is it that you do not fall into emptiness?
The Master said, "All things, such as words and letters, arise from wisdom. When the Great Function manifests before one, how could one fall into emptiness?

Kongming said, "Therefore, we know that if one does not penetrate even a single dharma, one cannot be called Siddhārtha. The Master said, "The Vinaya Master has not only fallen into emptiness; he is furthermore..."

Ming misunderstood the terminology and asked, "In explaining *rūpa* as 'form,' where is the error? The Master said, "If you have not yet distinguished between the Chinese and Sanskrit sounds, how can you lecture on it?
Ming said, "I request the Chan Master to point out the specific error. The Master said, "Do you not know that *Siddhārtha* is a Sanskrit term?
(*Siddhārtha* means 'One Who Has Accomplished All Meanings' in Chinese. Although Ming recognized his mistake, his mind remained indignant, and he spoke again.
"The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras are the words of the Buddha. One recites them and practices according to their teachings; why then do you not see your nature?
The Master said, "It is like a mad dog chasing a clod of earth while a lion bites a man. [The student asked,] "Are the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras the functioning of nature?
Is the one who recites them the dharma of nature? The Master said, "Does Amitābha Buddha have parents and a personal name? The Master said, "Amitābha's surname is..."

Thus ends the biography of the Great Master Wanshou. May all beings attain enlightenment through this merit. Sarva Mangalam!
At Wanshou Zhengzong Chan Temple, the Master was titled Great Master Miaojue Zhenkong.
When the seat at Songxi Puzai became vacant, the community requested the Master to preside over it. Upon ascending the hall, he expounded upon the fundamental tenets of Yuanweng;

his exchanges of question and answer were sharp and incisive, leading the assembly to regard him as possessing the spirit of the ancient patriarchs. He ascended the hall and said: "Fu fu fu! Mo mo mo! A mistake!"
"Wrong, wrong," he said, looking at his attendant and calling out, "Is this old monk’s tongue still there?
In the third year [of the Yuan era], he retired to Tianbao Ruiyun Pagoda Monastery. His dharma-heir, Shanchou, took charge of the monastery's affairs.

Although the Master lived in seclusion, the shoes outside his door were constantly full, yet he never grew weary of receiving visitors. In the eighth month of the sixth year of Zhizheng (the Gengchen year), he manifested a slight illness.
On the thirteenth day, he wrote a letter bidding farewell to Jingzhai and others. On the fifteenth day, after finishing his bath, he wrote a verse which said:
"Fundamentally there is no coming or going; a single phrase is fully raised. Crimson clouds pierce the azure void; the white sun circles Mount Sumeru. Having cast down his brush, he passed away.
His secular age was sixty-three and his monastic seniority forty-five. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Ruiun-in.

Two collections of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) have been transmitted to the world. Among the master’s disciples who received the Dharma, Shanchou and Zhishun both succeeded him in residing at the mountain monastery;
Zhishun has a separate biography.
During the final years of the Yuan dynasty, the ancestral style of the school had become sparse and silent. Nevertheless, there were still several individuals who preached the Dharma in Jianzhou;
Tieguan was among those who excelled. His recorded sayings (yulu) still survive today; like refined gold and pure jade, they stand out as naturally noble.
Those who possess discernment should treasure this for themselves.
△ The Chan Master Gumei Zhengyou of Gaoyang Mountain in Jianyang was a native of the Ding family of Guixi in Jiangxi.
Having left home at a young age, he took Master Benshan Ben as his teacher. Later, he traveled throughout Jianghuai and the two Zhejiang provinces to study under various masters.
Shi was once urinating when he touched the ground and attained a point of entry. Later, he requested instruction from Master Cheng of Prajna.
Cheng asked, "Whom have you previously requested instruction from? Shi replied, "I requested instruction from Master Haiyin, who taught me to hold up the word 'Mu'."
Cheng said, "How do you bring up the word 'no'? He replied, "Before it is brought up, it is already clearly understood. After several rounds of question and answer, Cheng said, "Stop for a moment.
Sometimes there is first illumination and then function; sometimes there is first function and then illumination.

When Lingyun saw the peach blossoms and attained enlightenment, Xuansha said, 'How perfectly accurate! How perfectly accurate! yet I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate. Furthermore—
Daoxuan asked Xuefeng, "Do you approve of him or not? Xuefeng replied, "I approve him at the very moment of his words. Cheng laughed heartily and said, "Neither before nor after is it right;
come back and see me again. The next day at the fifth watch, he went to the abbot’s quarters. Cheng asked, "What about last night's matter?
He replied, "Lingyun caught the thief; Xuefeng did not let go of the stolen goods. Now, thief and goods are both decisively returned."
The Master took up his sitting mat and struck him. Cheng asked, "What was the meaning of Huangbo’s sixty blows to Linji?
The Master then shouted. Cheng asked, "Why did you strike Daoyu three times with your palm, and then come back to strike Huangbo again?"
As soon as the Master opened his mouth, Cheng said, "It is not. The Master asked, "Ultimately, which one is it? Cheng then struck him across the head.
The Master again prostrated himself in full ceremony. Cheng said, "Go for now and come back to see me again. The next day at the fifth watch, the Master went to the abbot’s quarters.
Cheng said, "Pull out your *kāṣāya*. As the Master hesitated, Cheng struck him three times. The Master then let out a shout. Cheng struck him sixty more times.
The Master then ceased speaking. After the morning gruel, [the student] went to the Abbot’s quarters to request to reside there. Cheng said, "Go first to see Wuyong, Zhongfeng, and Duanya;
once you have done so, come and live with me. He added, "It will not do any harm to look through one or two lines of the *Dichang Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Dichi).
At that time, while staying at Bore for three days and three nights, his body and mind were as unsettled as a great...
It was as if he had been afflicted by a fever. Later, upon visiting Yunyan and reading the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) of Fachang, he encountered the passage:
"Driving the plowman’s ox; seizing the hungry man’s food. Suddenly, there was a moment of total penetration (*checuo*), and he was unaware that sweat was pouring from him.

He then composed several verses on *gong'an* cases and sent them to Cheng. After Cheng finished reading them, he said to the assembly: "This man has received the vital power of my third bamboo staff. However, he still..."
A fragment of the shell remained. When the Master heard this, he once remarked of himself, "What further shell remains to be shed? What further shell remains to be shed?
Another three years passed; while passing through the dining hall, he struck his alms bowl, and upon hearing the sound, he was startled and suddenly attained great enlightenment.
He then set out to visit Wuyong and subsequently studied under several other venerable masters before returning to his native village to settle in a thatched hut.
Longku (Dragon Cave) left [his previous residence] to reside at Tianxin Temple in Pucheng. He subsequently took up residence at Gao’ang Mountain in Jianyang.
The Imperial Preceptor memorialized the Emperor, requesting that he be granted purple robes and a monastic title. His initial title was Zhanran Zhiyuan; later, it was augmented to Furi Guangzhi.
When he manifested his passing, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Fengshan. Two volumes of his recorded sayings were transmitted to the world.
△ Chan Master Daegui Jeong-jang of Mount Dufeng in Yuan-Ōning was a native of Fúqīng, Fúzhōu.
He traveled to Tiānwáng Temple in Húnán to pay respects to Master Jeoljeong, where he shaved his head and received full ordination.

Desiring to investigate the "Great Matter" (the fundamental cause and condition) of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he first visited Xī West Hall in Guǎngzhōu, who expounded the essentials of the Dharma for him and directed him to visit Master Hwa of Donghae in Zhexi.

I further requested instruction on the methods for upward progress. At that time, as soon as I applied myself to practice, I felt it was effortless; yet, I simply did not know where the point of realization lay.
Reflecting on myself, I thought my karmic consciousness was too dense, so I would daily bathe my mind and repent before an image of Avalokiteśvara.
One day, Hai asked me, "How is your practice going now? I replied, "In my daily life, I have no interruption in the *huatou*; however, I am only..."
"No," said Hai. "Now is precisely the time for you to exert yourself. From this point forward, redouble your diligence.
Be restless day and night, as if you were in debt of a million strings of cash. Examine and investigate it again and again until you are utterly at a loss.

Suddenly, hearing Hai’s verse on Kūṭi’s pointing of the finger, he said: 'Profound and bottomless; high and beyond all grasping. The more one reflects, the further it recedes; the more one seeks it,' " he continued.

Again he was challenged. Upon hearing the words, he attained sudden enlightenment and proceeded to the abbot’s quarters. Guishan asked, "What is it? He replied, "The reality of the past and present is already perfected;
why must one engage in deliberation? Guishan said, "If you do not engage in deliberation, why have you come?
He replied, "I ask the Master to bear witness. Guishan asked, "To bear witness to what? The Master then gave a shout. Guishan said, "Where did you see Zhaozhou? He replied, "A mistake."
Haikui asked, "What did you say just now? The Master replied, "Mount Sumeru leaps. Haikui said, "Where is Zhaozhou right now? The Master replied, "He is not here.
Haikui said, "Why is Zhaozhou’s nostril in my hands? The Master replied, "I thank the Master for providing this witness.
Haikui said, "I grant you thirty blows of the staff; now give me back the verse on the word 'Not' (wu). The Master offered this verse: Dog.
"The seed of Buddhahood does not exist; look closely and the eyes wither. In a flash, he turns his body over: *Oṃ sili sulu*. Hai then patted him and sealed him.

Later, he built a thatched hut on Mount Doufeng, where it gradually became a monastic community. Entering the hall, after a long silence, he said: "Though gold is precious, once it enters the eye, it becomes dust.
He then descended from the seat. Entering the hall again, he said: "The jade palace is clear with frost; the emerald groves shed their leaves."
"Directly and completely upheld; ten thousand functions are stilled. Those who act as masters love to seek medicine for those who are not ill.
[The Master] descends from his seat. Entering the hall, he cites a monk’s question to Zhaozhou: "When the myriad dharmas all return to One, where does that One return?
Zhaozhou said, "I was making a cotton shirt in Qingzhou that weighed seven pounds. The Master said: "In the third watch of last night, the rain soaked the void. The tabby cat..."
"Knowing or not knowing, he climbs up and stands on the tip of the tree branch. On New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall and said: "The first day of the year begins the reign; all things flourish.
To call this 'the Buddha-dharma of the New Year' is to blind your eyes. Not to call it 'the Buddha-dharma of the New Year' is to cut out my tongue.
After all, what is it? Thereupon he descended from his seat. Later, when departing this world, the Master spoke a verse, saying: "Birth is originally..."
There is no arising; there is also no cessation. Since illusory transformations come and go, what use is there for discrimination? "Great assembly, take heed! It does not reside in words.
Having spoken thus, he joined his palms and entered nirvana.
△ Yuanjian Yang Yun’an Qing Chan Master: His dharma heirs are unknown. He resided at Jing Mountain in Hangzhou and served as the twenty-ninth patriarch.
A monk asked Yangqi, “What is the Buddha? Yangqi replied, “A three-legged donkey prancing on its hooves.
The monk said, “Is it not this very thing? Yangqi said, “Elder of Hunan. The Master then composed a verse: Yangqi— (Note: The verse itself is omitted from the source text provided.)
A single-headed donkey, its eyes flashing like lightning, tramples all people underfoot. What need is there to speak of three legs?
△ Yuan Songxi Fuxing was a disciple of Chan Master Song of Shaolin; his dharma lineage is unknown. He resided at Jingshan in Hangzhou.
He served as the thirty-third patriarch. A monk asked Muzhou, "What are words for unfolding and displaying? Muzhou said, "Appointing to office according to one's talent.
The monk asked, "What are words that do not unfold or display? Muzhou said, "I humbly pray you will accept this offering.

The Master said, "Muzhou was an ancient Buddha who skillfully responded to the stimuli of those who came before him. Nevertheless, even so, he only attained eighty percent. Or, if someone were to ask about the direct path..."
Shan asked, "What are words of exposition and manifestation? [Baizhang] immediately said to him, "To ask ten and answer a hundred—what difficulty is there in that?
Shan asked, "What are words that do not involve exposition or manifestation? [Baizhang] gave a shout and said, "Do not call this a cesspool! The Buddha spoke again.
He broke down the eastern fence and struck down the western wall; beneath the mountain gate, there was no standard at all. Who understands this?

He saw through the Sangha Hall and looked into the Fragrant Accumulation Kitchen; the *chīwén* (roof-ornament) bit off the ridge of the Buddha Hall. His ten volumes of recorded sayings were destroyed by fire.
△ Chan Master Zhishun of Nicuan at Tianbao Mountain in Yuan-Ōuning was a native of Ruian, Wenzhou. His surname was Chen;
his father was Daoxian and his mother was Lady Lou. Having repeatedly suffered the loss of children, she fashioned an image of Zhiyi (Zhizhe) and served it with devotion.
One night, she dreamed of a monk with a halo upon his head who ascended the river against the current. The monk beckoned to Lady Lou, saying, "I shall become your son."

Upon waking, she found herself pregnant. The child born was endowed with excellent qualities from birth; he did not delight in keeping his hair long, but possessed a transcendent air that seemed to belong beyond the mundane world.
The Lou family could not retain him, and at the age of seven, he was sent to rely upon his uncle Huiguang at the Chongxing Vihāra.

When he had grown somewhat older, he received full ordination at Tianning Chan Monastery. Thereafter, he traveled extensively through the lecture halls of various monasteries, where his reputation for brilliance became particularly prominent.
Eventually, he sighed and said, "While the study of doctrine (yixue) is beneficial, it merely increases one's learning; it cannot withstand the cycle of birth and death.

If one wishes to withstand birth and death, setting aside the nature of self, what else could possibly be clarified? He then changed his robes to enter the practice of Chan and went to Tianbao Mountain in Min to study under Master Tieguan Shu.

Zhushou bestowed upon him the essential points of the mind, instructing him to follow and practice them. When [the student] seemed to have a gradual sequence of stages and wished to abide by them, Zhushou rebuked him, saying:
"A man of great character does not compete with others within a vast forest; why confine yourself within this narrow snail shell?"

He brushed aside his sleeves and entered. The Master went down to the guest quarters and wept bitterly. Someone, feeling pity for him, comforted him, saying, "The gate of a true teacher is high and steep;
his rejection of you was actually an invitation for you to advance. When Shu heard this, he laughed and said, "I merely wished to test him. He then invited the Master into the hall.
The Master stood firm like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, showing no wavering or yielding; even though it was bright by day and dark by night, he remained unmoved.
He was able to discern it. Over a month later, while returning from using the toilet, he looked back at the garden and was suddenly triggered by a melon, which awakened a wondrous faculty.
His four limbs felt light and clear, as if he had just emerged from a bath. Light radiated from every single pore, and the great earth before his eyes suddenly sank level.
Reaching the pinnacle of joy and fortune, he hurried to the abbot’s quarters to seek verification. Just then, Master Shu entered the city. The Master did not...

He went to visit various masters, yet the karmic conditions with all of them were incompatible. Hearing that Master Chang Qianyan was proclaiming the Way at Fulong Mountain, he went there to seek instruction;

however, their exchanges were all confined to the path of intellectual reasoning. He returned eastward in a state of detachment, burning his finger to compose a vow, which he inscribed in small characters upon his sash, vowing not to rest until he had realized the Way. Later, he further reflected that this was insufficient without the "pivot."

He followed him and traveled repeatedly to Min Province, where he finally met him. When Huizhu happened to go out for a stroll, he saw the Master from afar and said with joy, "My son has come at last!
On the following day, the Master presented his realization to seek certification. Huizhu said, "This is merely entering the gate;
the Supreme Vehicle lies ten thousand miles away. He then instructed him, saying, "You must completely cast aside all your previous understandings."
If you apply yourself exclusively to the effort of inquiry and questioning, you will naturally enter the innermost depths. The Master followed this advice for over five months.
One day, as the evening session was about to begin, he was about to leave his seat when suddenly he attained a sudden awakening; it was like the clarity of empty space, impossible to grasp or fix.
He then cried out in a loud voice to Zhishu, "The failure of Nanquan has now been seen! Zhishu said, "No."
“This mind is neither Buddha nor an object; what is it? The Master said, “Bricks are laid on the ground;
tiles cover the roof. Zhushu asked, “Where is Nanquan right now? The Master said, “A hawk flies over Silla.
Zhushu said, “Wrong. The Master also said, “Wrong. Zhushu said, “Wrong, wrong. The Master performed a prostration with his head touching the ground. Zhushu said, “Not yet. Zhushu [departed].

Donning his great robe and ringing the bell to assemble the congregation, he proceeded to re-examine him. The Master smiled and said, "Before you have even uttered a word, we are already not on the same level.
Where are your eyes, Master? Are you performing this scene of theatrical drama again? Zhishu replied, "I also wish for the entire assembly to know.
He then questioned the Master one by one on the essential sayings of the Chan school. The Master answered each point in full detail.
Shu was impressed by him. After some time, he was ordered to take charge of the keys to the storehouse. Soon thereafter, he requested to share the seat with Shu to preach the Dharma.

Once Shu had passed away, the Master succeeded him in overseeing the monastery’s affairs. Not only did he uphold the shouting of the Chan school, but he also fully restored all aspects of the temple regulations that had been incomplete.
A brick-paved road led to the mountain gate, extending six or seven *li*. [The Master] chose a site to build a pavilion to enhance the scenic beauty, upon which the community relied;

yet he suddenly abandoned it and departed. He left the pass to travel through the Jianghuai region and returned to Wenzhou, where Wang Huaiqing of Ruian established Baoen Monastery on Mount Dulong and invited the Master to preside over it. Not long after, Wu Dedai of Pingyang began its construction.

He returned to Guiyuan Temple. Master Yuan assisted him in founding the monastery. The imperial court bestowed upon him a dharma robe, the temple plaque, and the honorary title "Fóxìng Yuánbiàn" (Buddha-nature Perfect Eloquence).
After some time, he completely distributed all his robes and alms-bowl accumulations. He retired to a single room, where he dug into the earth to make a hearth.

He broke off bamboo to fashion chopsticks; his demeanor was serene and unassuming. When Bianzhang Yanzhi was departing from Hua to serve as governor of the Fujian province, he passed through Dong’ou to pay his respects to the Master and inquire about the Way, specifically the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.

Delighted, he said to his attendants, “The masters of India transmitted secret meanings to me, yet I could not fully harmonize them. Now, having heard the words of Nichuan, my mind and heart have been opened and enlightened.”

He immediately called for his fellow passengers to enter Min Province and invited the Master to reside at Dongchan Monastery in Fuzhou. In less than a year, he renovated the old structures and established new ones, making them as if they were divinely fashioned.
Suddenly, he dispersed his wealth as if returning it to its source and withdrew in tranquility. Although the Chancellor Bianzhang tried to detain him, the Master did not comply.
When Xuefeng Monastery was vacant, the authorities forcibly requested the Master to fill the position. Upon arriving there, the Master went about rectifying its decay. Thus it was.
As he was thinking of returning to Wēn, Fang Canzheng prepared a boat to welcome him. Coincidentally, the Qianfo Monastery had suffered a fire, and there was no one to restore its ruins.
When the Master arrived, within the time it takes to snap one's fingers, the Qianfo Pavilion was completed.

Later, the Chan Master Lanyin of Jiangxin wished to build a Wanfo Pavilion, but being advanced in years, his strength was insufficient for the task; he consequently entrusted the project to the Master, who accepted it as well.

It was completed in no more than a few days. At the beginning of the Hongwu era, an imperial decree summoned ten monks of high conduct from Jiangnan to Mount Zhongshan to establish an Unrestricted Dharma Assembly (*amogha-saṃbhoga*).
The Master was among their number. He ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, and several thousand people attended.

The Imperial Carriage arrived in person, and the consolations bestowed were exhaustive; he was thus called the most favored of his time. Upon the completion of the rites, he returned south to Qiantang.
When Master Wei of Qingyuan retired from Jingci Monastery, he nominated the Master to succeed him. The Master accepted the command and went there, intending to establish great achievements.
Just as he was about to do so—
The imperial court summoned a monk of realized virtue to the capital to serve as a consultant. The assembly unanimously recommended the Master.

Upon arriving in the capital, he had been there for only four months when, after bathing and writing a verse, he passed away on the twentieth day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Hongwu era.
On the twenty-first, his body was cremated at Mount Jubao, where countless *śarīra* relics were obtained; these were taken back and used to construct a stupa.

It was stored there. The Master’s *Recorded Sayings* in Five Assemblies (*Wuhui yulu*) in several volumes and the *Verses on Sudhana’s Fifty-three Pilgrimages* (*Shancai wushisan can jie*) in one volume were both transmitted to the world.
Nichuan first resided at Tianbao, but after a short time he left; subsequently, he returned to his original residence at Dongchan.
Those who resided at Xuefeng all acted in this same manner. To disperse one's wealth and retire from office while one’s influence is at its peak—can this not be the mark of a great man?
Formerly, in the Song dynasty, there was one known as a "great master" who could not bear to part with even a single courtyard;

there were also those who, having already retired, could not endure the solitude and longed to return to their posts. Judging by these cases, such behavior is contrary [to the way of a true practitioner].
Sōgen was a teacher of ten thousand generations; it is a pity that his recorded sayings (*goroku*) have not been transmitted to the present day.

The commentary states: "The single dharma of Zen permeates all vehicles (*yāna*), yet all [other teachings] involve cultivation and realization (*shushō*) and thus fall within the realm of conceptual measurement (*karyō*).

Only Dharma’s direct pointing to the one mind is forcibly designated as 'Zen,' wherein there is nothing to be said regarding cultivation, realization, or conceptual measurement. It is just like a wheel..."
The King’s Topknot Jewel is supreme and noble; no other treasure can rival it. It is like a consecrated prince who, though still in his swaddling clothes, cannot be equaled by court nobles.
It is also like the sword of the Vajra King, which wields life and death with total mastery and cannot be constrained by conventional rules.
Therefore, those who are monks must prioritize this above all else; were they to abandon this for other pursuits, [they would fail their purpose].
Thus, even those who practice asceticism for accumulated kalpas will ultimately fall halfway; this is not a skillful method.
My own tradition was established in the Tang dynasty when Mazu first opened the gate of ambrosia. Since then, the transmission of the lamp has continued, its flames shining brightly everywhere.

More than forty people have entered the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp); as for officials, laypeople, farmers, and village women, they too have been able to partake in the flavor of the Dharma.
To enter together into the Mirror of the School—how magnificent this is! Toward the end of the Great Tang dynasty, the study of Chan declined;
yet Tieguan emerged late in life and still possessed the spirit of the ancient patriarchs. Is he not truly one who stands out with a brilliant resonance amidst the iron?

In recent times, Huilin has long been withered and the authentic lineage has already been lost; those who study Chan are few and far between, and even among those who claim to possess knowledge, there are but one or two.
Those who understand this must realize that they have all been taking a servant for their master and mistaking a rat for a jade treasure;
thus, it would be better not to do so at all than to act in such a way. Alas! The azure waters and crimson mountains remain as they were ten thousand ages ago.
Looking up and down, leaning upon the railing to offer my lament, how can I bear such desolation? It is here that I feel a profound sense of regret.
