Manifestation and Transformation, Part Two (totaling seventeen individuals).
Through the accumulation of sincerity, the profound stillness revolved, and spiritual responses manifested spontaneously. This is truly inherent and does not rely on anything external.

It is unfathomable to both sages and ordinary beings, and its modes of concealment and manifestation are boundless. In gathering and transforming sentient beings, this is the most extensive. [This concludes] the section on Manifestation and Transformation.
△ During the Tang Dynasty, there was Master Ai, whose name was Shou, of Mount Tongbo in Chong’an. His family was poor and he made his living as a farmer.

He served his mother with the utmost filial piety, showing no fear of cold or heat. Whenever he plowed in the scorching sun, clouds would invariably form to cover him. He subsequently built a hermitage on Mount Tongbo.

He moved massive boulders and great trees with his bare hands. He would sit cross-legged through the night without a mat, remaining upright until dawn. He was able to foresee the fortunes and misfortunes of others.

Whenever he administered water as a remedy for illness, even those with chronic and stubborn conditions were instantly cured. Sometimes people gave him four or five *shí* of rice, which he would carry away on his head.
When traversing dangerous terrain, he moved as swiftly as if flying. As he neared his passing, he informed the assembly and piled up firewood; then, he sat in the full lotus posture.
He sat and recited verses while setting himself ablaze. Amidst the smoke and flames, the sound of ringing bells and the chanting of sutras was heard without ceasing.

When the fire was extinguished, his remains were found intact, and several *liang* of *śarīra* relics were recovered. This occurred on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Bingyin during the Zhenyuan era. The local people fashioned a statue for him in a hermitage;
whenever they prayed during times of flood or drought, their pleas were invariably answered, and the villagers relied upon him for their well-being.
△ Chan Master Shenxuan of Jianyang during the Tang Dynasty was surnamed Liu by secular name. From childhood, he was silent and contemplative, speaking only when questioned.
While traveling as a guest to Wunü, he entered Kaiyuan Temple and immediately resolved to leave the household life; accordingly, he submitted himself to the tonsure.

Not long after, the Prefect entered the temple to visit his master. Seeing that the master’s spiritual bearing was bright and refined, the Prefect looked at him several times and remarked, “This youth...”
Truly a vessel for transcending the mundane world, he was destined one day to receive the profound Dharma. Surrounded by a thousand followers, he attained the supreme fruit;
indeed, he was no ordinary vessel. Thereafter, the Master devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Koṭi-mantra* of the Seven Buddhas, continuing without ceasing from dusk until dawn.
Upon completing his reception of the precepts, he took up residence within a stone cave at the Hundred Homes Cliff on Mount Geumhwa, where he lived in the open air without constructing a hermitage.
The dhūta practitioner had no bed or couch; however, a divine being emitted purple vapors to cover him. From afar, he appeared like a solitary pillar rising from the mist.

This divine being would occasionally come to inquire after his practice. One day, with hands folded in reverence, he said, "The eastern peak of the Crimson Pine Cave possesses exceptionally sublime forests and springs;
you may dwell there. The Master accordingly requested to go and reside there, whereupon auspicious omens became even more frequent. (Zheng)
In the second year of the Yuan era, he met Chan Master Zhixian. Xian said to him, "I have heard that you, my elder brother, maintain such mantra recitation;

demonic affairs will surely arise. To extinguish the demonic armies, one must recognize the fundamental nature of the body. Once the fundamental nature of the body is realized as true, there is neither Buddha nor demon. Upon hearing this, the Master was suddenly enlightened;
principle and phenomena were both perfected, and the efficacy of his divine mantras increased twofold. One day, a divine being asked, "What does the Master require?"
"What is it? he asked. [The master] replied, "I am suffering from the bitter cold on the northern side of the mountain. The divine person said, "This is a minor matter.
That night, a clamorous noise was heard, and at dawn, a small peak was seen to have shifted.

In the eighth year of the Yuanhe era, Vice Minister Fan Yang took charge of the monastery and dispatched an envoy bearing incense, felt rugs, woolen cloth, and various vessels. The Master then distributed these entirely to the assembly. Subsequently...
The Secretary of the Palace Library, Wang Zhong, requested that the Master come to Dayun Temple to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon the assembly.
In the twelfth year, although the Minister Meng Jian of Pingchang earnestly entreated him from Kuaiji, he did not go. In the eighth month, he suddenly returned to his old mountain;
no one could fathom the reason. He soon manifested his passing at the age of seventy-six. His disciples enshrined his entire body and erected a stupa.
At their native mountain.
△ The two Chan masters Xiao and Yuan of Mount Dading in Tangpu City were men of unknown origin.

During the Huichang era, when an imperial edict was issued to suppress the monastic order, the two masters retreated into Mount Dading and sustained themselves by gathering wild vegetables, such that no one knew of them.
Qiu Liangju, Duke of Liangguo, lived at the foot of a mountain. While by the water’s edge, he repeatedly found vegetable leaves;
finding this strange, he followed their source and saw two masters sitting in meditative repose beneath a pine tree. Suddenly, two tigers rushed forward, their roars shaking the earth.
When he was about to seize it with his hands, the Master called out, "Do not alarm my lord of the earth. The tiger immediately became as docile as a domestic animal;
it bowed its head and withdrew. The Master marveled at this extraordinary event and subsequently relinquished the land to establish a monastery, naming it Datong Temple.
△ During the first year of the Jingfu era, Chan Master Xingru of Zhongfeng Mountain in Songxi, Tang, was dwelling in a hermitage on the mountain.

At that time, there was a tiger that had bitten a person. The local villagers gathered a crowd to capture it, but the Master rode the tiger out to meet them. The multitude was greatly astonished and amazed.
For this reason, he was given the sobriquet "Subduing Tigers.
△ During the Five Dynasties period, there was Chan Master Kōubing Zhaogu of Ruiyan Temple in Chongan. He was a native of Xinfengli in his own prefecture.
His surname was Weng; his father, Chengzan, served as a Censor-in-Chief during the Tang dynasty. His mother, Lady Meng, one night dreamed of an old man...

A bhikṣu, radiant as a wind-god, carrying his staff and almsbowl, came to seek lodging for the night. A bystander pointed him out, saying, "This is a pratyekabuddha. Subsequently, she became pregnant.
On the eighth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Huichang era of the Tang dynasty, she gave birth;

an extraordinary fragrance filled the room and did not dissipate for an entire month. At the age of thirteen, she sought to leave the household life. Her parents, knowing her intention, found it to accord with her dreams.

He did not dare to detain him by force, but instead sent him to serve under Master Haengjeon at Heungboksa Temple on Eusan Mountain. In the year *Eo-woo* (1465), he passed the scriptural examination and received ordination;
he later received full precepts (*upasampadā*) at Bokdang. Initially, he was sought after by the assembly for his lecturing and exegesis.

One day, while traveling, he encountered an extraordinary monk who spoke to him regarding the principle of realizing one's nature (*jō-seong*), saying to him: "Your spiritual practice shall realize the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment]. It was no mere coincidence.
"The various stages of dhyāna can be categorized; you should exert yourself in them. From that time on, he abandoned his former studies and devoted himself exclusively to the contemplation of dhyāna.

After a long period, his realization reached its ultimate limit. One day, he said to his teacher, "What is the difference between merely guarding a single mountain valley of white clouds and traveling to view the bright moon over a thousand rivers?
Now I have heard that Xuefeng is called a great master of knowledge (mahājñānin); I request permission to go and see him. Thereupon, he set out directly.
Xuefeng built a snow hut. Xuedou took a bundle of *fu-ci* (water chestnuts) and a jar of sauce and presented them to him.
Xuefeng asked, "What is in that bundle? Xuedou replied, "Water chestnuts. Xuefeng asked, "Where did you get these? Xuedou replied, "I got them from the mud. Xuefeng asked, "How deep is the mud?
Xuedou replied, "It is several *zhang* deep. Xuefeng asked, "Is there more? Xuedou replied, "The deeper one goes, the more there is. Xuefeng then asked, "And what is in the jar?"
Wu said, "Sauce. Feng asked, "Where did you get this? Wu replied, "I made it myself. Feng asked, "Is it cooked yet? Wu said, "It is more than cooked enough.
Feng marveled at him, saying, "In the future, you will surely become a teacher to a king. After staying for several days, Wu took his leave and returned to his former hermitage.
Not long after, he once again took up his staff and left the pass to visit Ehu; upon returning to Wenzheng Peak, he then established a meditation hut there.
He resided there (later becoming Yongbong-sa). He subsequently dwelt at General Rock (Janggun-yeok), where two tigers were constantly by his side.

One day, a divine being knelt and petitioned him, saying, "This place is frivolous and unsuitable for a holy master to reside. At the foot of Mount Suyeon (Seogwang-san) is a place where tigers have run—a site fit for a great Dharma center.
I pray that you, Master, will go there to settle the great assembly. The following day, he cleared away the brambles.
He entered [the mountain] and, having attained the stage of fruition, eventually moved his staff there. He founded Ruiyan Monastery, and students vied with one another to return to him.
The Master said to the assembly, "The practice of the ancient sages must rely upon austere discipline. Now, in summer I wear coarse cloth, and in winter I strike the ice to bathe.

Thus, the common people called him the "Ancient Buddha Who Strikes Ice," and his reputation for the Way grew even more prominent. At that time, Jianyang suffered from a severe drought. The district...
Lord Tonghui requested the Master to pray for rain. The Master wrote a verse and cast it into the dragon pool, saying:
"O you, the undulating one! Listen to my Dharma words. The Way of Heaven favors life; how could it allow the grain to wither? You preside over this pool—why are you so stingy as to withhold the rain?

Now that the appointed time has passed once more, the Dharma shall not forgive you. In an instant, black clouds gathered from all sides and a great rain poured down like a torrent. The assembly was greatly delighted.
The following year, Huì requested the Master to reside at Lingyao Temple. As the Master ascended the seat, he said, "The fourfold assembly has gathered like clouds;
what can this old monk say? He then descended from the seat. A monk piled burning charcoal into a shrine-like niche and said, "We pray that the Master will enter here to practice.
The Master replied, "True jade does not follow the flowing water; lapis lazuli vies with the multitude of stars for its brilliance. The monk said, "Do not merely..."
"It is just so," the Master said. "But do not mistake the servant for the master. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "A lotus blooms in the twelfth month.
In the second year of the Tiānchéng era, the Prince of Mǐn, Yán Hòu, sent a special envoy to invite the Master. The Master went to the capital at the Prince's request.
The Regional Inspector, Chén Huì, had built Xiǎnqīn Temple; he had fashioned weapons into Buddhist statues, and once they were completed, he offered them a meal.
There were one thousand monks. He requested the Master to offer them a verse of praise. The Master said, "A thousand-year-old piece of rusted iron becomes a Buddha in a single morning.
Huì was greatly pleased; indeed, "Rusted Iron" (Chéntiě) was Huì’s childhood nickname. He then asked, "Among the monks I feed, is there no extraordinary person?
The Master replied, "There is none. Huì asked, "How might such a person be obtained? The Master said, "I shall bring one for you. The next day, he again prepared a vegetarian feast. There was—
An old woman leading a black dog arrived from outside; the Master descended the steps to receive her and invited her to take a seat at the head of the assembly.

When she had finished her meal and departed, Huì asked who she was. The Master said, "Do not ask. Huì pressed him for an answer, to which he replied, "This is the Bodhisattva Water-Treasury (Jiaozhi Pusa) leading a black dragon.
When the Master reached Fuzhou, the King came out in person to welcome him into the city and provided him with lodging in the government offices by the water.
At the pavilion, the King bowed twice and said, "I thank you, Master, for descending from afar. As they sipped tea, the Master lifted up his bag and asked, "Does Your Majesty understand?
The King replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The Human King and the Dharma King each reflect upon themselves.

The King was greatly delighted and invited him into the palace, personally offering him purple robes and vestments as gifts. The Master said, "I thank the King for his kindness; I shall stay for only ten days."

He remained. He entreated the Great King, saying, "I pray that you will keep the common people in mind and refrain from killing many. He stayed for ten days and then took leave on the pretext of illness.

The King personally escorted him out to Mount Gu. On the second day of the twelfth lunar month at the hour of noon, after completing his ritual bath with incense, he ascended the hall, addressed the assembly, and passed away.
His worldly age was eighty-five and his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*) was sixty-three. On this day, the clouds darkened the sky and the birds’ cries filled the wilds with sorrow.
He remained in his physical form for seven days, his complexion as if alive. The King used fragrant wood and clarified butter to cremate him, obtaining countless relics of five colors.
The King erected a stupa at Saeok (Auspicious Rock) and enshrined the Master’s remains in the main chamber, naming it "Saeok" (Auspicious).
As for the "Responsive" (Ruiying) stupa: he further placed a golden vase containing the śarīra-relics at the site of the cremation; this was also called the "Auspicious Response" (Ruiying).
He was posthumously titled Great Master Miaojue Tongsheng. During the Song dynasty, his posthumous title was successively changed to Great Master Fawei Ciji Miaoying Puzhao.
The divine wonders manifested when he struck the ice are exceptionally remarkable; there is no doubt that he was a pratyekabuddha reborn.
Nevertheless, when I, a fool, examine the words of his teachings, they are not something a pratyekabuddha could have accomplished.
△ Chan Master Wugou Pusu of Nanzen Baoying Temple in Ou Ning during the Five Dynasties period was surnamed Huang.
He was a native of Min County, Fuzhou. At the age of twenty-five, he left home to become a monk at Xishan Yi Temple in his home prefecture.
Later, he studied under Chan Master Xuefeng Cun and attained the essential meaning of the Buddha-dharma. He traveled to Jianzhou, where the Chancellor Zhang Zhongya...

He held [the Master] in high esteem and subsequently donated his residence to establish a monastery, naming it Nanzen Bōō-in (Southern Zen Baoying Monastery). He invited the Master to serve as its first patriarch.
In his later years, the Master declined the affairs of the monastery and traveled with his staff to the Chan cliffs, where his spiritual wonders became increasingly manifest.

Once, while cultivating a field at the foot of Shuangji Cliff, the field was completed but lacked water. The Master used his staff to strike the mountain, causing it to split open and thereby channeling water through it.
He irrigated the fields, and even today these superior traces remain. On the third day of the tenth month in the second year of the Tiānchéng era, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
His worldly age was sixty-three, and his monastic seniority thirty-nine. He was posthumously granted the title of Great Master Huìmíng Pùzhào;
the local people enshrined his portrait and worship him, and his spiritual responses are as swift as an echo. He is titled the Ancient Buddha Wúgòu.

△ Chan Master Haiju Daozhen of Tianshin Temple in Pucheng, Song Dynasty. His origins are unknown. He once recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until he entered into a state of clear, resonant realization.
When the assembly requested him to reside at Tianshin Temple, one day by the bridge over the Nanpu River, he discovered a single scroll of commentary on the *Vajracchedikā*.
He immediately entrusted it to Ge of Jieshou to have it carved for publication. Prior to this, Ge...

One evening, he dreamed that a monk urged him to publish the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The next day, the Master arrived, exactly as he had dreamed. He began to regard this as extraordinary.

When he was about to pass away, he informed the assembly, saying, "On such-and-such a month and such-and-such a day, I shall return. On the appointed day, he bathed, changed his robes, sat upright, and entered nirvana.
He identified himself as the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati. His stupa was erected on the side of Huanghua Mountain behind the monastery.
On that day, thunder and lightning crashed violently; people said it was a "thunder burial.
△ During the Song dynasty, at Fuxian Temple in Jianyang, there was a Venerable Wang named Fachang. He was originally from Dongtian in the same prefecture.

Having lost his father in childhood, he devoted himself to filial care for his mother. During the Qingli era, he shaved his hair to become a *dhūta* and entered Fuxian Temple, where he applied himself diligently to arduous practice.

He suffered. He would not pull up living grass nor cut down living trees. His body was covered with many lice and nits; he frequently turned them over and rearranged them so that they might all be equally satiated.
Everyone ignored him. In the *Xinhai* year of the Xining era, he told people, "I shall depart next year. No one believed him.
In the fifth month of the following year, on the eighteenth day, he passed away while sitting in meditation without illness. The local people were then struck with wonder and marvel.
He was posthumously granted the title of Great Master Cijie (Compassionate Precepts), and his physical body remains preserved to this day.
△ Yao Shengzhe, courtesy name You’an, of Fuxian Temple in Jianyang, Song, was a native of Changxi, Fuzhou. In his youth, he studied Confucian arts;
in his maturity, he took the tonsure at Guanyin Temple in Guangzhou. In the *Renzi* year of the Xining era, he arrived at Jian [Mountain], where he encountered the passing of Great Master Cijie.
He composed a verse in praise of him and remained at the mountain’s base. Desiring to construct a bell tower, he traveled to Wuxian himself.

He traveled by mountain to solicit offerings, departing in the morning and returning at dusk; the distance calculated was one hundred and twenty li. The old bell tower was dilapidated, and no one dared to ascend it.
The Master climbed the ladder to release the bell as if walking on level ground. Liu Chaofeng of Wufu came to the mountain to pray for progeny.
The Master said, "I shall give you a son, Yao Dian. He will be born on such-and-such a day, month, and year; his name may be Yao Ge. When the appointed time arrived, it was indeed as predicted.

Throughout his life, he acted with eccentricity, using his madness to confound the worldly people, such that no one recognized him. In the first month of the Bingchen year of the Xining era, he bathed, adjusted his robes, and passed away.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master Ciji (Compassionate Aid). His physical body remains preserved to this day.
△ Chan Master Daowu of Qingtian Rock in Ouning, Song Dynasty. A native of Qianxi in Sanyuan, his surname was Zu.
In the Jiazi year of the Yuanfeng era, he went to visit Chan Master Ying of Kaiyuan Temple in Jianzhou. Master Ying showed him a verse, which said:
"Master Zu could not read characters; The Patriarch likewise was thus. Writing is quite ordinary, Yet body and mind are inconceivable. The Master understood the verse.

He attained realization and subsequently sought ordination. He remained in dependence [upon his teacher] for over ten years. Later, in the year Wuyin of the Yuánfú era (1118 CE), he built a thatched hut at Qíngtiān Rock in the western district.
There he practiced pure cultivation with austere discipline, performing the *dhūta* ascetic practices.

In the year Dinghài of the Dàguān era (1107 CE), as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he announced the date to the fourfold assembly. When the appointed day arrived, he shaved his head, bathed, changed his robes, and spoke this verse, saying: "I am born..."
It is thus. Death is also thus. This side and that side have never been two. Water cannot soak it; fire cannot break it. Hehe! What is this?
It is precisely what is meant by: "That which passes away is like this [river]. When the verse was finished, he sat within the stupa and underwent cremation.
It was the twenty-first day of the first month. The Venerable Xian collected the remains and fashioned a statue in the hermitage. Far...
Those who prayed to him in recent times received responses as swift as an echo. In the sixth year of the Caoshun era, bandits were rampant; the imperial troops were cut off from their food supplies.

The Master manifested himself and went directly to the military headquarters, identifying himself as the Abbot Qingtian (Supporting Heaven). Carrying a single bag of food, he provided for all the soldiers' needs.

Consequently, they attacked the rebels and defeated them decisively. The authorities reported this to the throne, and he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master Jigan (Quiescent Response) and bestowed with [imperial honors].
The inscription reads: "Supporting Heaven and Protecting the Nation. It was composed as a record by the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Mr. Xie Die-shan.
△ During the Song dynasty, Chan Master Zu-jian Cong-mi of Ruiyan Monastery was a native of Tingzhou. Having studied under Master Le-tan Qian, he attained the essential instruction.
In the sixth month of the sixth year of the Xuanhua era, the Chief Censor, Mr. Wu Yan-guo, invited the Master to reside at Ruiyan. Prior to this, [he had] sought...
Yunben went to Min at the request of its Prince. At Songmen, he took leave of the great assembly, saying, "Two hundred years from now, this old monk shall return again to sweep the hall.
When the Master arrived at Ruiyan and reached Dongling, he had a sudden realization, saying, "I have returned to this place.

He struck the ice [to test it] and retrieved Yunben’s discarded *kāṣāya*, which was over a zhang in length; when the Master donned it, it fit him perfectly. Judging by the prophecy at Songmen, it was indeed two hundred years.
Baian opened the hall and said: "Opening one's mouth is not Chan; closing one's mouth is not the Way. If you step forward with intent, your whole body will fall into the wild grass.
Later generations established Chonglai Hermitage on the eastern ridge to enshrine him there.

△ In Song-dynasty Jianyang, there was the Rushi Hermitage (Rushi Ān), where Master Ji, whose name was Cunzhen, resided. A native of Shuiji in Ouning, he initially established his hermitage at Chongyuan in Jianyang.

He was devoted to the practice of *dhūta* (asceticism) and took pleasure in farming and tilling. Whenever he went out, he acted according to his spontaneous will, making no distinction between self and other.
During years of drought, he would call out, “Rain! and rain would immediately fall; when it rained excessively, he would call out, “Sunny! and the weather would immediately clear.
When the sick arrived, they were cured instantly upon drinking the water. In the *Xinhai* year of the *Shaoxing* era, he went directly into the deep valleys of Lianyuan.
A deity welcomed him, saying, "I have waited for the Master for a long time. Thereupon, he halted his staff and established a hermitage, naming it "Thusness" (*Rúshì*).

On the nineteenth day of the sixth month of the *Ren-shen* year, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. For ten days his body did not decay, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room. Thereupon...
It was fashioned from fragrant clay. When rain and sunshine were irregular and locusts ravaged the crops, prayers for divine response were answered like an echo.
During the Zhizheng era, he was bestowed the title Great Master Dingying Tongjue Huizhao Shanying. Every year in the sixth month, those who flocked from all directions were as numerous as clouds;
the flourishing of his incense offerings and lamps was preeminent within Fujian. In common parlance, he was called "Old Buddha Ruyi."
△ Chen Gong of Fayun Hall in Jian’an, Song Dynasty: His origins are unknown. He once built a hermitage on Mount Fayun and employed a tiger to carry out his tasks;
his divine anomalies were widely renowned. Later, he moved to Lion Rock in Zhenghe. Without prior illness, he requested a bath, and having finished, he donned his robes and passed away while seated.
Today, there is a testament left at Fayun which says: “On the day the Southern Kingdom is restored, it shall be the Shaoxing era.”
The year was established; clouds parted as the original hall was founded. There have been times of prosperity and times of ruin. One fire left behind a gateway; two fires constantly feared the sun.
In the year Bingyin, fire arose; in Jihai, six people arrived. There was a man wearing yellow, riding an ox amidst thunderclaps.
I had already known this long ago: flying clouds passed to the far west. In a dream, I asked about dwelling in error; it was by relying on this that [the disaster] was avoided.
I established this place with great care. This man was able to read books; we accompanied one another for nine months. Yet, during the first watch of the night, he harbored two minds.
To open the mountain, it must be done with urgency; leave behind only the man surnamed Li to reside in the center and act as my steward.
△ Song’s Incense-Selling Old Lady of Songxi was the daughter of the old man Chen of Haotianli. From her youth she had never married and made her living by selling incense.
Whenever she had leftover incense, she would invariably burn it at the foot of a cliff; sometimes she would stay overnight on the cliff, abstaining from food for several days.
People considered her to be insane, yet only Li Wulang of the village always treated her with respect. One day, having returned from selling incense, she called out to Wulang.
When Bi Wulang arrived in pursuit, [the monk] had already transformed and departed; Wulang then ate the remaining rice and likewise transformed and departed.
People subsequently named that cliff Xiangpo Rock (Fragrant Wife Rock).
△ Yuanzhenghe: Chan Master Huikong Yuemo of Jiangshan. He was a native of Longchu, Gutian. His secular surname was Su;
his father was Yuancai, and his mother was Lin. Initially, when his mother had not yet borne a son, she prayed at the shrine of the Divine Lord Liu Zhenji Xianyou.
One night, she dreamed that the deity called out to her, saying: "Mother, I shall become your son. However, ten years hence, you must return to my lineage."
Having finished speaking, he immediately transformed into an infant. His mother woke up in surprise and subsequently conceived.

He was born at the hour of the rat on the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the year of Yimao of the Baoyu era of the Song dynasty. He was thus named Shenqi. As soon as he was able to speak, he joyfully recited the names of the Buddhas.
After paying his respects, both his parents passed away. He became a foster son of the Liu family in Shuocun, Shuiji, Ouning, where he lived as a sojourner.

At that time he was only eleven years old, which precisely coincided with his dream of returning to his ancestral clan ten years later. Whenever he heard someone reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he would immediately seek to learn its practice and recitation;
he could chant it fluently like a flowing stream. At the age of fifteen, he was abducted by the Wu Thousand-Household Commandant and taken back to Pucheng.
He was further taken in by one surnamed Liu. The following year, he received the precepts of refuge at Jixin Hall.

At the age of nineteen, hearing that Master Hai-zhu at Hou-shan Tang in Jianyang was renowned for having attained the Way, he went there to study under him. The master instructed him to recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion.
He practiced walking meditation day and night for three months without ceasing, and subsequently attained the Pratyutpanna Samādhi. Later, while at Pucheng...
Jingshan again encountered Wu Qianhu. Seeing that the Master was extraordinary, Wu apologized for his previous transgressions and offered him gold and silk.
He personally escorted the Master to Wanshou Temple, where he took the tonsure and received full ordination under the Venerable Puqin, who changed his name to its present form.
Puqin instructed him in the practice of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Consciousness-Only). At that time, he was twenty-seven years old; it was the year of Xinsi in the Yuan Zhiyuan era.

The Master had already cultivated the contemplation of Consciousness-Only and profoundly realized the two kinds of emptiness. He practiced the six perfections in unison and simultaneously applied the four means of integration.

Wherever he was, he established skillful means to guide and lead others. Once, while soliciting donations at Jianyang to carve woodblocks for the *Lotus Sūtra*, he produced and distributed five thousand and forty-eight copies.
Some remarked that it was inappropriate to engage in such conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). The Master replied: "How can you know that he who is occupied with these all day long..."

"Have you ever eaten a single grain of rice without chewing it? I have heard that Śākyamuni Tathāgata has enshrined eighty-four thousand volumes of the great scriptural treasury within the bodies and lives of eighty-four thousand sentient beings;
thus, within the body and life of each such being, there exists the full number of these scriptures. I now vow, regarding the bodies and lives of such sentient beings..."
From within [the earth], he extracted such a scripture-scroll and revealed it to sentient beings, making it fully manifest.
Thereafter, he caused these sentient beings to attain Buddhahood simultaneously. The Venerable Gengzi arrived at Dongpingli during the Zhenghe era;
there was a man named Jiueying who was also by nature fond of the Buddha. He spoke with the Master of the excellence of Mount Jiang and said, "This is truly a place for salvation and manifestation."

This is the place where the Divine Lord Liu You manifested himself. Upon hearing this, the Master immediately realized his karmic connection from past lives. He entered meditative absorption and traveled spiritually to Jiangshan.
Jueying also dreamed that he ascended Jiangshan with the Master, arriving at the site of Chan Master Xuanjiang’s monastery.
There was an elderly man of very ancient appearance who came forward to greet them, saying, "I have guarded this mountain for five hundred years. Having finished speaking, he transformed away.
The Black Dragon flew away. Beside the Master stood a man in attendance, majestic and peerless. The Master asked him, "I am Zhang Shiji from Waterji;
since the Master first arrived at Ruo Village, I have served as your guard, never for a moment leaving your side for thirty-five years.
When Jueying awoke, he related this in full to the Master. The Master merely smiled, and after a while said:
"I shall return to my origin and restore the source upon this mountain. Jueying then built a hermitage for him.

On the first day of the seventh month, he sat in the lotus position and entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*). After two weeks had passed, on the fifteenth day, he finally emerged from absorption and said to the assembly:
"In the presence of the Buddha, I was known as the Bodhisattva Huikong. Now that my karmic conditions for transformation are exhausted, I shall immediately enter *nirvāṇa*. Because of this—
For the sake of the assembly, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and further recited three verses. The first said: "For over forty years I dwelt amidst the secular dust;
Now, at last, I manifest the Honored One within this very midst. A night wind arose from the east upon the crag; It blew the blossoms open, filling the tree with spring.
The second said: "The iron boat has neither rudder nor sail; Punted into the nature-ocean of the golden lotus. At the very end..."
Ji now spoke to shatter [their delusions]: "The white clouds have never been separate from the vast sky. Thirdly: "Mountains and rivers across the great earth leave no trace when sought;
when empty space is struck through, the ultimate reality is seen. Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one's head, the original nature’s perfect luminosity is never lost.
Having finished the verse, he further addressed the assembly, saying: "The third patriarch of the Western Heaven was the Venerable Śāṇakavāsa."
In the past, at Mount Bālasvabhūti, he manifested the Dragon’s Vigorous Display Samādhi (*nāgavikrīḍita-samādhi*) to preach the Dharma and subdue the various assemblies of non-Buddhists.
Thereafter, he transformed himself into fire and consumed his own body. "I shall now do likewise while dwelling before the Elephant Trunk Rock. He then entered the Dragon’s Vigorous Display Samādhi.
At that time, clouds and mist gathered from all sides and thunder and rain broke forth violently; subsequently, he transformed himself into fire and consumed his own body.

His physical stature was [imposing]. His worldly age was forty-six and his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*) was twenty. The assembly collected his sacred remains and erected a stupa to the west of the hermitage;
they also fashioned a statue within the hermitage. After he entered the stupa, a circular halo would occasionally flash forth, witnessed by many.

To this day, there is no prayer or rite for the distant or the near that does not bear immediate fruit. Every year in the seventh month, those who come to pay their respects are very numerous; all address him as "Hui-."
Regarding Master Kong Pusa:
he was born on Mount Jiang and was endowed with spiritual wonders; he is undoubtedly the Bodhisattva Hui Kong. Yet, how is it that he came from within the realm of the divine?
Might the Divine Lord Liu also be a manifestation shown by the Bodhisattva? This final passage of light...
His brilliance remained exceptionally outstanding, such that the fourfold assembly turned toward him like gathering clouds.
△ Ming Shouning was the Daoist Jin Han of Hupian Hermitage; he was a native of the Ninth District of this prefecture.

During the Xuande era, at the age of thirty-two, he entered Hupian Hermitage to cultivate the Way. He refined his conduct through austere asceticism without the slightest sign of weariness. In the second year of the Hongzhi era...

In the tenth month of that year, on the fifteenth day, he was about to pass away. He had previously arranged with his fellow villagers, who lived at distances of sixty to seventy li from one another, to visit him all at once in person.
When the appointed time arrived, he ascended the wooden funeral pyre; he then plucked out the wick of a lamp himself, and smoke and flames rose up in all directions.
The body and the stupa were both consumed by fire. After a short while, a single monk’s sandal was cast down from mid-air.
This practice of burning the body is permitted in the Mahāyāna but prohibited in the Hīnayāna.

The intention is that in the Mahāyāna, because the weight of compassionate vows is profound and the power of forbearance is already sufficient, it may be permitted. Those who permit it do so perhaps to make offerings to the Great Dharma and thus perform the act of burning.
Some burn [themselves] to protect the Great Dharma, while others burn to preach the Great Dharma; their benefit is thus immense.
In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), however, the emphasis on self-interest is heavy and the aversion to suffering is profound; their urgent desire to burn themselves yields but meager benefit.

How much more so for those whose power of forbearance (*kṣānti-bala*) is not yet sufficient; fearing that they might lose their right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) when facing peril, how could one possibly enumerate the harm such a state would bring?
Furthermore, there are in this world those possessed by demons, those who act out of greed for posthumous fame, or those who act out of self-aggrandizing provocation.
Once right mindfulness is lost, one will inevitably invite evil retribution, lightly entering the ranks of ghosts and spirits and sinking deeply [into the realms of suffering].

"Abhi! Should this not be prohibited? In this collection, it is recorded that after Duke Ai’s transformation, several *he* of *śarīra* were obtained, and a golden mendicant cast down a monk’s sandal from mid-air. There is no doubt that these could be burned.
However, I fear that ignorant people might recklessly imitate such acts; therefore, I have not seen this as being permissible."

The treatise says: In the study of the Śākyas, the Way (mārga) is the root, while supernormal powers (abhijñā) are the branches. The Dharma dictates that one must prioritize the Way; once the Way is perfected, supernormal powers will spontaneously manifest.
If one’s intention is set on seeking supernormal powers, one will inevitably lose the Way. To lose the Way while gaining supernormal powers is the work of Māra;
how much more so when even those powers are eventually lost? Therefore, one with right view would rather attain the Way than possess supernormal powers. This is not [the case for others].
This refers to the penetration of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*). Such a dharma cannot be pursued through effort. Furthermore, there are generally five ways in which this penetration is attained:
there are those who attain it by practicing the Mahāyāna; those who attain it by practicing the Hīnayāna; those who attain it by practicing the vehicle of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-yāna*);
those who attain it by practicing the teachings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); and those who attain it as a karmic retribution resulting from past cultivation. Thus, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ.

The correct [classification] is also different; they cannot be generalized and equated as one. For instance, in the cases of Ruiyan Koubing and Jiangshan Huikong, these were ancient sages manifesting their traces, and there is nothing to be doubted therein.

As for those such as Duke Ai and his peers, some attained only partial minor fruits, some remained stuck at the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), some fell into the ranks of ghosts, some emerged as external adherents, and others were perhaps great-power bodhisattvas (*mahopāyaka-bodhisattva*).
Since there are these various distinctions in the skillful means used for gathering and transforming beings, they cannot be indiscriminately suppressed, nor can they all be equally extolled.
Laypeople certainly lack the capacity to discern this; however, those who study the Way ought to know what their primary concern should be.
If one merely sees these extraordinary traces and gives rise to delight, one will surely drift toward heterodoxy without realizing it. Is this not something to be deeply cautioned against?
Section on Revering Virtue, Part Three (Total: fourteen individuals).
With extensive learning yet modest benefit, they practiced reality and achieved merit. Eye and foot mutually supporting one another, they reached the subtlest depths.

Embodiments of sagacity and vessels of purity, they trod the path of benevolence and soared with wisdom. To look up to them and gaze upon them is to find a model for a thousand years. This is the Section on Revering Virtue.

△ Chan Master Jianyang Mingjue of the Tang Dynasty was surnamed You. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations. He was refined and elegant in character, possessing a deep reserve;

he delighted in inquiry and seeking knowledge without ever growing weary or indolent. Having long harbored a spiritual nature, he heard that Chan Master Daoyi had begun his teaching at Fojiling in his native district.
He thereupon went forth to receive the tonsure. After some time, carrying his staff, he traveled to observe the various quarters, extensively tasting the flavor of the Dharma. Later, he visited...

At Mount Jing, he applied himself with earnest intent to seek resolution. For several summers, he carried firewood until his face was sunburnt and his hands were calloused. Descending the mountain, he went to Dayun Temple in Hangzhou to observe the *jinzu* (retreat).
Subsequently, he moved to reside atop Mount Qing at the edge of the lake. Lu Zhongcheng of Fanyang, having heard of his reputation, came to pay him homage.

He went in person to invite the Master to reside as abbot at Dayun Temple. In the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era, seeking to avoid suspicion and distance himself from clamor, he withdrew to Mount Tianmu, where he lived in a thatched hut.
In the spring of the third year of the Changqing era, Shanxin constructed a monastery for him.
When February of the following year arrived, a great drought broke out; wild fires spread and were about to reach the monastery. The assembly was all terrified, but the Master said: "I and..."
A forest fire on this mountain was about to break out, but it was quickly extinguished. Shortly thereafter, thunder and rain broke out suddenly, and the fire was completely put out.

People from near and far were struck with wonder and turned toward him in unison. On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Taihe era, he manifested his passing into nirvana.
△ Once, the Venerable Bian Cong of Jianyang, Song, traveled to a monastery on Mount Wutai. The senior monk (upādhyāya) of that monastery was elderly and held in low esteem by the assembly;

however, the Master alone treated him with reverence. As the Master was about to return to the capital, the old monk gave him a letter and instructed him to seek out Bohe north of the city and deliver it to him.
The Master took his leave and departed; he secretly opened the letter to read it, but found no other words in it except for the single character: "Du" (to ferry across).
"Sentient beings have already come; they have already come. If you stay any longer by force, I fear you will create further karma. The Master was greatly startled and again sealed it up.
When he reached the banks of the Guangji River, he heard a young boy calling out "Bohe. The Master asked, "Where is Bohe?
The boy pointed to a large pig with a golden ring on its neck, lying beneath the wall to the west of the street. The Master knocked on the wall and questioned it.
"To whose house do you slaughter? He replied, "To the home of Mr. Zhao. He asked, "What is the name of this pig?
He replied, "Because it eats only *bóhé* (coriander), the children of the village call it by that name. I slaughter hundreds and thousands of pigs every day;

when the other pigs bolt and are difficult to drive, I use this pig to lead them, and they follow one after another to their death. I have kept it for fifteen years. The Master then presented his letter.
Bohe hurriedly ate, whereupon he suddenly stood up and passed away. The old monk was a sage.
While the multitude all held him in contempt, Cōng alone revered and served him. Was it not because Cōng was one of the Sage’s followers?
Bohe’s deeds—extending his compassionate transformation upon the wheel of blades—were made possible solely by relying on Cōng.

I have circulated this for the sake of its dissemination. Is it not the case that one who possesses such discernment belongs to the ranks of the sages? Therefore, I have carefully recorded and transmitted it.
△ The Dharma Master Zhìrán of Chōng’ān during the Sòng dynasty was a native of Zhōu Village. His surname was Chéng.

He applied himself with rigorous austerity to the study of the classics, gaining a profound mastery of their abstruse meanings. Possessing quick wit and eloquence, he required no further editing of his compositions. He once traveled to the capital, where the high officials put him to the test.

When he composed commentaries and treatises, his brush moved with such spontaneity that they were completed on the spot; the assembly marveled at this and praised him. During the Hongfa era, he propagated the Dharma in the capital, where the multitude hailed him as "Yitiger" (Tiger of Meaning).

Later, by imperial decree, he traveled to India to retrieve scriptures, returning with a stone cauldron. He used it to boil medicinal decoctions for treating illnesses, achieving cures without exception.
Upon presenting himself before the Emperor, his responses pleased the sovereign, who bestowed upon him purple robes and the title Liaokong (Emptiness Realized).
△ During the Xining era, Chan Master Jingkong of Nampeongsa in Songpu resided in seclusion at Baekhwaryam Rock.

Having awakened to the essential meaning of Chan from his youth, Zhang Heng, the Court Attendant for Ceremonial Rites, invited him back to Nampeong. Later, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.

Upon cremation, several śarīras were obtained and enshrined at Sangyunam Hermitage behind the temple. By imperial decree, he was posthumously honored with the title Grand Master Huiying. (Recorded by Zhen Xishan)
I have compiled this record.
△ Song Dynasty, Yunju Monastery in Chongan: Master Sisi was a native of the same prefecture. In his youth, he studied Confucianism and served as a disciple of Master Hu Wuding.
Later, he abandoned Confucianism to enter the Buddhist path, shaving his head at Yunju Monastery. He transcended worldly affairs and was deeply immersed in the joy of Chan meditation.
Wendeng sent him a poem, saying: "For ten years, north and south, we have been like severed geese and fish. In dreams, I long for the man atop Mount Yunju.
Can you truly satisfy yourself forever with fragrant food? You should surely share it to sustain this body of mine for a hundred years."
△ Chan Master Ken’an Yuanwu of Kaishan Temple in Chong’an, Song Dynasty, was a native of Jian’an.
His understanding and conduct were highly esteemed by all, and Zhu Xi (Hui-ang) held him in profound respect. He once composed a poem on plum blossoms in response to Hui-ang’s own, which read:

“Pitifully, after ten thousand trees have withered away, / It stands firm amidst the bleakness of wind and frost. Those who heard it could not help but praise it. On the day of his passing into *nirvāṇa*, Hui-ang... [text fragment ends]
I wept and composed this poem: Once parted from the human world, all things become empty. Incense burned and tea steeped, I lament our meeting.
There is no need to transform the thirty *shí* of earth; The twelve peaks, purple and green, pierce the heavens.
△ Yuan Jian’an Bāiyún Chóngfàn Sī Yūsǒu Chénjiàn Chánshī was the son of Zhāng Shùshí of Níngdé County.
From an early age, he admired the Buddha-vehicle and strictly abstained from meat. At the age of fourteen, he left home to rely upon Master Qīyún of Lóngshān Sī in Zhènghé County.
Qīyún shaved his head and conferred the precepts upon him. Subsequently, he traveled extensively throughout the rivers and lakes to seek instruction.
Venerable Master Wumen Can of Jianfu Temple in Ruzhou subsequently entered his [the master’s] quarters.
At that time, Chancellor Guxin Jiang Gong, Qingshan Zheng Gong, Zhongshu Pingzhai Hong Gong, and Dianshan Xie Gong all resounded with the Master’s profound transformation.
Later, he was invited by a provincial edict to reside at Baiyun Monastery in Jianzhou.

When Zhitisi was destroyed by bandits during the twentieth year of the Yuan Zhizhi era, Emperor Shizu issued an imperial decree the following year for the Master to serve as its abbot. He rebuilt the monastic buildings.

In the second year of the Dade era, he was granted the title Great Master Tongwu Mingyin. On the fifteenth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Zhida era, a divine being appeared and said:

He manifested his traces in the Western Region (India). The Master then wrote a verse, saying: "For eighty-two years, I have been deceived by worldly conditions; now, with a somersault, I manifest my traces in the West.

On the nineteenth day, he bathed, changed his robes, and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Throughout his life, the Master had been upright and incorruptible, neither taking nor giving improperly.
He was majestic yet not fierce, clear-sighted yet not scrutinizing. His bags contained no superfluous goods, and his room was [devoid of excess].

He was a man of extraordinary refinement. Whenever he passed through monasteries, he would never so much as cast a glance at those who were not practitioners of the true lineage. He ordained more than eighty disciples.
△ Chan Master Gudede of Hujing Hermitage in Jianyang, Ming Dynasty. A native of Jiyang in Ouning, he showed no interest in worldly affairs from his youth.

He consumed meat during his youth, but as he grew older, he yearned for the Way. Having heard that Master Guxin was the direct descendant of Zhongfeng and the eldest son of Qianyan, he went to rely upon him and subsequently requested ordination.
The moon of his precepts and the water of his concentration together nourished his spiritual sprouts; the light of his compassion and the flames of his wisdom mutually adorned his Dharma-nature.
During the Hongwu era, he traveled to Junting in Jianyang, where he built a thatched hut to live in seclusion on the mountain for three years.
The ground was parched and lacked water, so he set out to leave. A fierce tiger stood across his path, striking its head against the ground. The Master brushed it away, but it did not move.
The Master said, "Do you wish to detain me from my journey? The tiger rubbed its forehead against his. The Master said, "I am leaving because I lack water; can you provide it for me?
The tiger then took the Master’s robe in its mouth and returned to the mountain, where it used its claws to dig into the earth.
A spring gushed forth spontaneously, its water clear, cool, and sweet. The Master then returned to reside there, and it gradually became a Buddhist monastery (*brahmacarya-śālā*).

On the third day of the eighth month in the *Bingwu* year of the Xuande era, at the hour of the Ox (*chou*), he passed away while sitting peacefully without illness. He was one hundred and one years of age. A *stūpa* was erected on the mountain where he lived.
None of the Master’s Dharma discourses have been transmitted; there is only a poem that says: "Stream clouds brush the earth, sending off the remnants..."
It rains; valley birds cry out toward people as fallen flowers drift by. It is also said: "Ten thousand li of azure clouds unveil the evening hues;
a single silver river stretches across the autumn sky. Observing this, one can sufficiently perceive the lingering grace of the Master.
△ Chan Master Zutong of Donglin Monastery in Chong’an was a native of Jiangxi. His surname was Jie.

Having renounced Confucianism for Buddhism, he traveled extensively among the lecture halls of various monasteries. Later, he entered Min Province and took up residence at Donglin Monastery in Chong’an.

Although the Master was thoroughly versed in the Three Vehicles, he made the Pure Land Dharma-gate his primary goal. The local magistrate, Lord Jin, held him in high esteem. The *Zhengtong* year, Ren... [text continues]
On the eleventh day of the eighth month of the *xu* year, he bathed, changed his robes, and wrote this verse: "The source of the mind is profound and still; cease your restless seeking.

With body at rest in a single room, ten thousand matters come to an end. Without the movement of arms or spears, home and state are peaceful. Heaven is long and earth is enduring—how many springs and autumns have passed!

Having finished writing, he sat cross-legged, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away. He was eighty-five years of age. His coffin remained for sixty days, during which time extraordinary [signs occurred].
The fragrance was rich and pervasive; both monastics and laypeople turned toward him in reverence, all sighing in admiration at such a rare occurrence.

△ Ming’ou Ning Dufengshan Dachen Huitong Chan Master, a descendant of the Shao clan of Zhenghe, took the tonsure and received full ordination at age twenty under Master Yuxi of Dufeng. Later, he first visited Master Zhou Shanzhu, who instructed him as follows:

The Zen Case of Nianfo (Buddha-Recitation). He went to Sujiyan to close himself in retreat for three years. One day, while sitting in meditation until midnight, he suddenly became completely oblivious to his own body;
only the *hwadu* remained vividly present without dispersing. Consequently, he was seized by great fear and felt restless day and night.
He left the retreat and went to Tianjie Temple in Zhenghe to consult Master Huizhong, asking: "I, this person, [find that] my eyes..."
Previously, he did not perceive the existence of a body, but was only aware that his *huatou* (critical phrase) remained undispersed. He asked, "I do not yet know what kind of state this is.
Huì replied, "This is when a person has forgotten the self but has not yet forgotten the Dharma. He asked again, "My fear does not cease; I do not yet know for what reason.
Huì said, "This is like a fledgling bird that has just left its nest in the tree: it cannot lift itself high into flight, yet it cannot go far away. Therefore, fear arises. However—"
Fear is he; fearlessness is also he. You need only now cast aside attachment to body and life and carry this practice with you.
After days, months, and years, the waters will become clear and the moon will appear; it will naturally become manifest.

Following these instructions, the Master returned to his former seclusion and applied himself from the beginning once more. After another three years, one night, in the blink of an eye, there was a sudden "keng" sound from the earth.

Having grasped the turning of empty space and realized that his entire being was without self, he went to visit Master Huihong at Mount Zhong. Their spiritual capacities and conditions accorded perfectly, and Huihong subsequently bestowed upon him a whisk and a *kāṣāya*.
In the spring of the *guisi* year of the Chenghua era, he left the mountain ranges to travel for study; in the autumn, he arrived in the capital, Beijing, where his reputation spread far and wide.
The eunuch Huang Gao petitioned the Emperor on behalf of the Master to establish a monastery.
The Emperor bestowed upon it the name Zhengfa Chansi. When the Master opened the hall for a general discourse, the fourfold assembly was greatly delighted.

In the winter of the Wuxu year, he took his leave to return to his native mountains. Later, he resided at Junfeng in Shaowu, where a single volume of his recorded sayings remains transmitted to the world.
△ Ming’ou Ning’s Dufengshan Guyin Jingqin Chan Master was the son of Cai of Jianyang.
At the age of twenty-five, he took leave of his mother and went to Dongfeng Hermitage to pay respects to the Abbot of Chishishan and receive the precepts. That very evening, he asked:

The Master said, "People say 'clarifying the mind and seeing the nature. Is this not simply being aware as soon as one's own mind arises? The Master said, "This is the deluded mind, not the true mind.
To identify with this mind is to mistake a thief for one's own son. The Master asked, "If that is so, then am I without a mind?

The Master said, "It is you who know there is nothing known, and who are aware that there is nothing perceived. The Master [asked], "Master? (Note: This appears to be the Master addressing the other; however, based on the preceding dialogue, it may be a scribal error or a rhetorical device indicating the end of the exchange.)
Upon hearing this, he immediately and directly shed his body and mind. He alone beheld his own nature, which is neither knowing nor not-knowing, neither awakening nor not-awakening.
He subsequently lived in seclusion in the mountains for three years. Throughout his daily life, there was always a constant, luminous clarity that was never obscured;

it was simply a self-evident understanding within his heart that was difficult to express in words. Thus, he doubted whether his realization had reached its ultimate limit, and out of this resolve, he set out to travel to various teachers. First, he went to Jun...
Feng relied upon Master Da-chan for a long time, yet he attained nothing. Taking his leave, he traveled to Jiangle to visit Xingkong, the head of the monastery.
There he met Chan Master Jinghuang, and they subsequently went together to Shaowu. Along the way, hearing Huang describe the practice of *gongfu*, Feng was half-convinced and half-skeptical.
One day, while Huang was reading the *Record of Gumei*, he came across the account of a monk who visited the abbot’s quarters twice.
[The master] said, "So-and-so has attained a point of entry, but he was driven out by blows on two occasions. Huángxiào remarked, "This monk truly possesses a place of awakening;

it is simply that his Great Dharma is not yet clear. When the Master heard these words, he knew for himself that the Great Dharma was not yet clear, which is why he lacked the wondrous function of responding to stimuli.
Later, while sitting at night in a temple, [Huángxiào] leaned his body askew and asked, "Brother Teacher, you..."
"Tell me, from where does the practice of cultivation begin? For example, when creating worldly objects, from where do they arise?
What is their waist? Where is their completion? Only when there is such a metaphor will I believe you. Huáng said, "It is precisely because of such questions that I can speak to you.
Generally speaking, everyone possesses Buddha-nature; it is only because one lacks the wisdom of the Buddha that it remains obscured."

To eliminate afflictions, one must ensure that the conditions for awakening do not fail to coincide; otherwise, one will fall into the mire of worldly sentiments, which those with true insight would never willingly accept.
It is like the worldly process of brewing wine: although there is rice and water, it is essential to employ the power of the yeast (*maku*) to ferment and transform them.

If the power of the yeast does not act upon them, wine will ultimately not be produced. Likewise, although humans possess Buddha-nature, if they lack the power of great wisdom, [enlightenment cannot be realized].
If one pursues transformation through intellectual effort alone, one will ultimately fail to become a Buddha and shall remain nothing more than an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Generally speaking, those who apply themselves to the practice of *kung-fu* must cast aside all that they have held as right or wrong throughout their lives. They should take up a single phrase of their fundamental inquiry (*huatou*), subjecting it to self-doubt, self-questioning, self-pressuring, and self-pursuit.
They must not seek others to explain it for them, nor allow themselves to clarify it through conceptual interpretation; they must focus solely on the phrase itself.

Below this, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is suddenly severed with thorough mastery. In this way, pressed and driven three times by day and three times by night, as years pass and months deepen, suddenly one day there is no thought in the mind, yet one or two lines, four or eight lines flow forth from the mouth, responding to the occasion and hitting the mark.
This is called the realm of intelligence (*cōngmíng*). Generally speaking, those who awaken to the Way all proceed from the realm of intelligence.

This is a transcendence within the realm; it cannot be realized immediately. One must simply press forward relentlessly. Suddenly, one day, hundreds of thousands of verses may issue forth from the mouth at will.
One's entire body becomes the mouth; by all means, do not let go. This is precisely when you must exert effort. It is like making wine:

after the great boiling, one continues until the liquid has settled and cleared before stopping. When a person applies themselves to practice, they must pass directly through the realm of intellectual cleverness.
The realms [of reality] were fully realized; he thoroughly penetrated all one thousand seven hundred ancient kōans.
To the point where there was no Zen to investigate, no Buddha to attain, and no Dharma to doubt—every single thing was fully understood, and every phenomenon was completely permeated.
Whatever came from his mouth was entirely in accord with the standard. At that time, he understood for himself and did not cease until he was finished;

he rested for himself, like a person who has reached home and no longer worries about the road. Upon hearing these words, the Master felt as if he had obtained a great treasure. He immediately rose, prostrated nine times, and said:
"Had it not been for my elder brother's instruction, I would have spent my entire life in vain wandering the pilgrimage routes. From this point on, he [the Master] truly took up the practice.
Regarding the *kōan* "The Ten Thousand Dharmas Return to One": he returned separately to Longxing Monastery and resided on the mountain for three years.

Through rigorous training and the practice of *daqi* (seven-day intensive meditation), he pressed himself from all sides, asking, "Where does this 'returning to one' ultimately lead? He subjected himself to severe self-reproach. When the three-year term was complete, he went to Hangzhou to receive full ordination.
Afterward, he went to Baifa Temple to practice *zazen*, where he met the Venerable Sōmyō from Shizhou, under whom he repeatedly received exhortations and encouragement.
They then traveled together to Sichuan to visit Master Shoutang. On the way, they stayed for the winter at Guanyin Temple on the Jitan River in Nanyang Prefecture.
That winter, heavy snow fell fourteen times in succession, and few people were traveling back and forth. Day and night, he brooded over his doubt;
his entire being became a single mass of inquiry, free from even a hair’s breadth of distracting thought. Suddenly, one day, his mind was as if—
It is like the turning of a wheel. Taking up a public case that had previously been difficult to clarify, he resolved it on the spot.

One day, while casually observing an object before him, he composed a verse for each; this was because he recalled his elder brother Huáng’s description of the realm of intelligence, thinking, "Today is that very thing."

Again, two years later, he arrived at the Great Monastery on Mount Wu where he was able to meet Master Shoutang. He presented his realizations, and subsequently received the Master’s seal of approval (*inka*).
He then took his leave to return to Min, where he later resided at Mount Doufeng. There he rebuilt a great monastery and propagated the teachings throughout the region.
On the day of his passing, flocks of birds wailed mournfully throughout the night. When his reliquary casket was moved out through the main gate, the fish in the pond all leaped up several times.

Chich. Among those in the mountains, there were some who did not believe in the Master; upon seeing his extraordinary features at this time, they all shed tears and prostrated themselves before his stupa, gazing toward it.
He authored the *Tihé jí* (Collection of Essence) in three fascicles.
△ Chan Master Tianzhen Daojue of Doufeng Mountain in Ou Ning was a native of Qili in Jian’an.
His secular surname was Zhang. Having lost his father at a young age, he devoted himself to filial care for his mother. When his mother also passed away, he remained restless day and night.

He encountered a friend named Zongliang, who asked him, “The kindness of one’s parents is profound; how can it be repaid? Liang replied, “To repay such heavy debt of gratitude, nothing is better than leaving the household life.”
At home, he realized the mind-ground and felt that no kindness could ever be fully repaid. Upon hearing these words, the Master was greatly pleased.

The following day, he went with Liang to Rui Peak Temple to pay respects to Master Dayong Ji, who ordained him as a monk. Later, he was given the *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) kōan. Subsequently, he resided at West Peak Rock;
however, over the course of several years, his thoughts remained distracted and his focus on the kōan was inconsistent. He then went to visit Master Guyin.
Master Qin instructed him to contemplate: "The myriad dharmas return to the One; to what place does the One return? For several months, his practice was continuous and profound.
Suddenly one night, he no longer perceived body or mind, nor was there even the phrase [to contemplate]. He could neither advance nor retreat; filled with doubt and unease, he found no peace.
He then hurried to see Qin and presented what he had attained. Qin said, "This is merely a temporary cessation of thought; it is not great enlightenment.
He urged him to resume his diligent practice from where he had left off. Later, when Yan’an Anqi invited Qin to serve as the abbot, they went together to the Jiyuan Hall.
There, they applied themselves to their work day and night. Within one month, he entered meditative absorption twice and subsequently experienced a realization. He then composed [this verse]:
The verse says: One hand claps, one hand drums; the True Person of No Rank performs a dance beyond the ordinary.

From his mouth he sings a tuneless song; the three thousand Buddhas share the same mother. On the day of the scheduled dispersal, he presented this to the Abbot, who immediately conferred upon him the seal of approval.
Li Gongmo, the Minister of Personnel, had long admired the Master’s spiritual resonance and became a transcendent friend with him. Later, [the Master] resided at...
The reputation of Dufeng spread even further, and people vied with one another to take refuge in him. Wherever the Master traveled, favorable conditions gathered without exception;

consequently, he presided over the restoration of more than twenty monasteries of various sizes. Yet, as soon as each project was completed, he would depart, remaining entirely untainted by worldly attachments.
On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Longqing era, he passed away while seated in meditation. He was seventy-nine years old.

△ It is recorded that the Abbot Xingpumo of Jianyang Desheng Hermitage was simple and robust by nature. He had no other interests; he was not particularly proficient in the doctrines or principles [of the sutras], but devoted himself solely to the practice of Pure Land.
Daily, he recited the name of the Buddha thirty thousand times and also chanted the *Lotus Sūtra*. When he was about to enter nirvana, he experienced no suffering or illness from beginning to end.
For several days, only a rare fragrance was perceived. The Master said, "The conditions for my journey to the Western Paradise have arrived. He then bathed and changed his robes.
Clothed in his robes and sitting upright in meditation, he wrote this verse: "Foolish, deluded, and dull-witted, I, De Ying, have failed to recognize the Buddha-nature throughout my life.
Today, I shake off my sleeves and return to the West, shattering the perfect mirror of the Western Paradise. Having cast down his brush, he passed away with a serene expression.
Master Ying possessed neither many arts nor much wisdom; he achieved his success solely through the six-character mantra of the Buddha.

Yet, when one observes that single verse he composed at the time of his departure, was it not evident that he truly knew [the truth]? As the Sūtra says, "If the mind is gathered in a single place, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. How true this is!
△ Master Yunyang Dehe of Dongyan’an in Jianyang was the son of the Wan family’s Sangui. By nature he was pure and refined, untainted by worldly vapors.
He served his parents with great filial piety; once his father had passed away, he immediately resolved to transcend the world.
He studied the methods of refining the golden elixir. Once, while walking at night among desolate graves under a bright moon in the sky, he spoke these words to himself:
He said, "A body of a hundred years comes to an end and ultimately returns to this earth. Within this, there is an immortal person.

If you do not attend to him right now, you are merely a fellow carrying a corpse. Upon learning of his mother’s passing, he traveled extensively to famous mountains until he reached Songxi to study under Master Wangu.
Wangu instructed him with the *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha's name) *huatou* and directed him to study under Master Tianzhen Juegong."

Jue-shou [bestowed] upon him the profound purport of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. From this point on, the Master devoted himself single-mindedly to investigation and no longer engaged in the practice of cultivation.
He resided on Mount Yue for several years; maintaining the "head-word" (*huatou*) alone, both dullness and distraction were completely severed.

One day, after the rain had cleared, he was walking through the mountains when he saw people moving a wooden board across the wet ground. Suddenly, he attained realization. From then on, the profound meanings of all the scriptures were [clear to him].
He did not look through [to the essence]. In response to whatever questions were posed, he answered like an echo.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "The one behind you. The monk said, "Is this not simply it? The Master said, "Why do you want me to be so?
A monk asked, "What is it like when the black bean has not yet sprouted? The Master said, "It has been sprouting for a long time. Lin Longjiang of Putian first...
Yansheng considered himself a follower of the Three Teachings; wherever he went, the gentry and commoners alike revered him as a Buddha.
When the Master went to pay his respects, Yansheng stood in a row to receive him. Upon hearing the Master’s discourse, he was greatly astonished and marveled at him;

△ The Venerable Yuan-chang of the Yian-’an in Dongyan, Jianyang, Ming Dynasty, a native of Raoyou, abstained from meat and stayed far from desire from his youth, as if he possessed what is called the "inherent precepts" (*daoju jie*).

Yet, his deep investigation and solitary attainment in the study of Chan were likewise such as this; if so, how could Chan be detrimental to loyalty and filial piety?
